name: German Whist
description: German Whist is a two-player trick-taking game with a stock phase and an end phase. Early tricks are used to draft better cards from stock; only the second 13 tricks determine the standard hand winner.

overview.description: German Whist is a two-player trick-taking game with a stock phase and an end phase. Early tricks are used to draft better cards from stock; only the second 13 tricks determine the standard hand winner.

history.origins: German Whist is a two-player trick-taking game of British origin despite its name. It appears to have originated in England and was popular among diplomats in Vienna in the late 19th century. Rules were first published in London in Home Notes (1894) and in R.F. Foster's Encyclopedia of Games in America (1897).
timeline: 19th and 20th century: Popularized as a head-to-head Whist derivative.
Modern era: Commonly included in printed and digital two-player card collections.
history.cultural: Known as a tactical bridge between pure trick-taking and card-improvement games.
history.evolution: Main rule families differ on whether follow-suit is enforced in stage one and whether only stage-two tricks or all tricks count.

setup.players: Exactly two players; standard 52-card pack, ace high. Deal alternates after each hand.
setup.dealing: Deal 13 cards each one by one. Place remaining 26-card stock face down and turn top stock card face up; its suit is trump for the hand.

rules.objective: Win the majority of the 13 tricks in stage two after stock is exhausted.
rules.gameplay: Non-dealer leads first trick. For each trick, second player follows suit if possible in standard form. Higher card of led suit wins unless a trump is played to a non-trump lead. In stage one, trick winner takes the exposed stock card and trick loser takes next hidden stock card; winner then leads next trick. After 13 tricks, stock is empty and stage two begins with no replenishment. Play 13 final tricks; these determine winner in standard scoring.
keyRules: Trump suit is fixed by the initial face-up stock card and does not change.
Stage one tricks are for hand improvement, not usually for scoring the hand outcome.
Stage two is a normal closed-hand trick contest with 13 tricks.
Variant tables may count all 26 tricks or relax follow-suit in stage one.

strategy.basic: In stage one, avoid spending strong winners to collect weak exposed stock cards.
strategy.intermediate: Time trump expenditure to secure high-value exposed cards and deny them to opponent.
strategy.advanced: Plan stage-two shape during stage one by controlling suit length and preserving tactical entries.
tips: Evaluate each stage-one trick by card gain, not immediate trick count.
Track revealed stock quality and infer opponent hand upgrades from contested tricks.

variations.name: No Follow-Suit in Stage One
variations.description: Common variant allows any response card in stage one, while stage two uses strict follow-suit.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Stage-one follow-suit is a rule toggle; engine overrides not yet mapped for this variant.

variations.name: Count All 26 Tricks
variations.description: Winner is player taking majority of all tricks across both stages, not only stage two.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Variant changes which tricks count; scoring override for trick count could be added when implementing.

variations.name: Honeymoon Whist
variations.description: Related designed variant with extra modifications and jokers.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Related game with different deck and rules; overrides to be added when implementing.

scoring.description: Standard hand result is determined by majority of tricks in stage two (the final 13 tricks).
scoring.winCondition: Win more of the 13 stage-two tricks than opponent.

synthesis.shortDescription: Two-player trump trick game where early trick wins draft exposed stock cards and final tricks decide hand winner.

hero.title: GERMAN WHIST
hero.subtitle: Two-Player Whist
hero.tagline: Draft strong cards in stage one, win the final thirteen tricks.
